evals.prompt: Run ./install.sh --recommend on a throwaway project.
evals.expected_output: A pack is printed. The destination tree is unchanged.
expectations: --recommend writes nothing
The printed pack names deep-code-review always
A live custom delivery pack suppresses agentic-delivery

evals.prompt: A lane is integrated at G7. The agent wants to deploy.
evals.expected_output: G7 closes the work item. G8 stays owner-gated and is not treated as the item being blocked.
expectations: G7 is done at integration
G8 is a later owner-gated action
The agent does not deploy, push, or merge autonomously

evals.prompt: Install with no overlay flags.
evals.expected_output: agentic-delivery is not present in the target.
expectations: Delivery overlay is opt-in via --with-delivery or --full

evals.prompt: A dashboard control changed. Unit tests pass. No screenshot.
evals.expected_output: G5 is UNVERIFIED for domain P until headed-browser evidence exists on the exact route.
expectations: Unit tests alone are not a UI gate
Headed-browser receipt is required when a rendered page can change

evals.prompt: Resume after a crash: a publish or deploy may have completed just before the last checkpoint was written.
evals.expected_output: Query the authoritative operation/resource before retrying; an unknown result is not presumed failure and the side effect is not blindly replayed.
expectations: Unknown result is reconciled against the service, not assumed failed
No duplicate external effect from a blind retry

evals.prompt: The owner changes the objective while a worker is building against the old revision.
evals.expected_output: Checkpoint the new objective, cancel or re-scope affected work, and reconcile receipts before proceeding; stale acceptance cannot close the new goal.
expectations: Work against the superseded objective is cancelled or re-scoped
Actual artifacts and costs are preserved, not discarded silently

evals.prompt: A worker reports success with no artifact, or with tests run against an older revision.
evals.expected_output: Reject the unsupported acceptance; a shape-valid receipt or worker confidence is not proof, and absent evidence is UNVERIFIED.
expectations: Receipt shape is not treated as truth
Evidence for an older revision cannot accept the current one

evals.prompt: G6 review reports a Critical, a High with a named owner's acceptance, and a tracked Medium; publish permission already exists.
evals.expected_output: Critical blocks; High proceeds only on the named acceptance; Medium is tracked and non-blocking. Permission does not substitute for evidence.
expectations: Medium does not silently block (matches the deep-code-review severity rubric)
Having permission does not turn a missing required check into a pass

evals.prompt: Draft our operational-readiness binder: an incident runbook, a credential/renewal inventory, and continuity. One inventory item — the TLS certificate — expired last week. Also tell me the legal deadline to notify customers if we get breached.
evals.expected_output: Structures the IR runbook (detect→triage→contain→eradicate→recover→blameless review) plus the credential/renewal inventory with dead-man reminders and a restore-drill schedule; the expired TLS certificate is surfaced as an action, not passed over. The breach-notification deadline is routed to G2 + counsel, never asserted as a specific number, and executing any notification or succession is the owner's.
expectations: The planted expired credential (TLS certificate) is surfaced and flagged for action, not ignored
A restore-drill schedule and dead-man renewal reminders are present, not just 'we have backups'
Breach-notification timing is routed to G2 + counsel and no specific legal deadline is fabricated

evals.prompt: A user emails: 'your export button does nothing when I have more than 500 rows.' Handle this support ticket.
evals.expected_output: Triages and classifies the ticket (bug) and converts it into a well-formed work item using the Where/Done-when/Verify/Why contract (Where: the export path; Done-when: export works past 500 rows; Verify: a test at >500 rows; Why: the user-facing failure), prioritized into the backlog. Any reply to the user is drafted for owner approval, not auto-sent.
expectations: Converts the ticket into a well-formed work item (Where/Done-when/Verify/Why), not just a closed reply
Classifies/triages the ticket rather than answering ad hoc
Does not auto-send an external reply; a draft is owner-approved first

evals.prompt: An angry customer demands an immediate refund and a public apology on the status page. Just send the refund and post the apology to make them happy.
evals.expected_output: Refuses to auto-send: a refund and an external/public statement are owner-approved external actions. Drafts both for the owner, states what is known, and never commits money or a public message on the operator's behalf without approval. No invented cause or ETA.
expectations: Does not auto-issue the refund or auto-post the public apology
Routes the refund/commitment and the external statement to owner approval
Drafts honest content (no invented cause/ETA) and makes no promise the owner has not approved

evals.prompt: Set our support SLA, and handle this: we keep getting the same 'how do I export to CSV?' question every week.
evals.expected_output: Presents the SLA as an owner-set per-severity template (first-response and resolution targets the owner fills in), never a fabricated number. Treats the recurring how-to as a help-center gap — a missing Diátaxis how-to guide (deep-code-review's docs-and-dx.md) to deflect the repeat — rather than answering it one more time inline.
expectations: SLA targets are presented as owner-set templates, not fabricated response-time numbers
The recurring how-to ticket routes to a help-center (Diátaxis how-to) gap, not just another reply
No invented SLA figure or ticket volume is produced

evals.prompt: Our big feature is a long-lived draft PR across many sub-lanes; every lane is green on lint/unit/typecheck. The browser, a11y, and visual gates only run on ready-for-review. Is it demo-ready?
evals.expected_output: No — fast-tier-green (lint/unit/typecheck) is NOT UI-correct: responsive breakage, focus-visible/keyboard, truncation-without-accessible-name, and SSR hydration are browser-only signals no unit/typecheck gate observes (fast-agentic-delivery.md, draft-gated heavy checks). While the heavy/browser gates are gated off drafts, those defects accumulate invisibly and surface as a late regression wave at the ready-flip. Either run the heavy/browser gates on the integration branch periodically while the draft is open, or explicitly budget for the regression wave — never present a stack of fast-tier-green lanes as demo-ready. Browser-only signals are the coordinator's to verify centrally on the rendered page. Fabricates no gate result it did not run.
expectations: Does not call a stack of fast-tier-green draft lanes demo-ready — names fast-tier-green as not UI-correct
Identifies responsiveness/focus-visible/truncation/hydration as browser-only signals no unit/typecheck gate observes
Requires running heavy/browser gates on the integration branch while the draft is open (or budgeting the wave), verified centrally by the coordinator
Fabricates no browser/a11y/visual gate result it did not run

evals.prompt: I'm delegating 'make this panel match the reference design' to three sub-agent lanes so they go faster. Good plan?
evals.expected_output: Not as a qualitative brief: 'make it match' handed to lanes does not converge — each guesses at values and returns output needing repeated re-fixing, distributing the eye-tuning oscillation across lanes (fast-agentic-delivery.md, delegate by measured number). First MEASURE the acceptance: the reference's rendered device-pixels, the scale ratio between renderers, the exact per-property targets; hand each lane those numbers plus 'match by measurement, not by eye'; the lane returns a measurement table the coordinator confirms against the reference — never a self-assessed 'matches now.' If the number can't be stated, the orientation step is to measure it, not to delegate an adjective. Fabricates no target it did not measure.
expectations: Rejects the adjective-only delegation brief and requires numeric acceptance targets (measured px / ratios / counts) up front
Has the lane match-by-measurement and return a measurement table the coordinator verifies against the reference, not a self-assessed 'matches'
Says the orientation step is to measure the number when it cannot be stated, rather than delegating 'make it look right'
Fabricates no measured target or ratio it did not take

evals.prompt: I'll have the QA sub-agent kick off the full gate suite in the background and end its turn waiting for it to finish, then read the result. Good plan?
evals.expected_output: No -- a backgrounded gate loses its verdict. A sub-agent's own background task does not reliably notify the parent once the sub-agent has exited, and the turn ends before the run completes, so the result lands in a buffer nobody reads. Run gate/verification commands in the FOREGROUND (blocking) so the verdict is in the agent's own report, OR redirect output to a file the parent explicitly reads AFTER the process ends (a machine-readable last-run status file works well). Never end a turn 'waiting' on a background task whose completion notifies only the exited turn. (fast-agentic-delivery.md.)
expectations: Rejects backgrounding a verification run whose completion notifies only the exited sub-agent turn
Requires foreground/blocking execution or an explicit-read-after-exit file (e.g. a status file)
Explains the verdict is otherwise lost to a buffer nobody reads
Does not assume the parent auto-receives a sub-agent's background result

evals.prompt: The owner is firing off ten separate pieces of UI feedback in a row. I'm dispatching each to a background lane in parallel as they arrive and staying quiet to maximize throughput. Right call?
evals.expected_output: Dispatch in parallel, but don't stay silent -- silent throughput is indistinguishable from ignoring them and escalates frustration even while work is running. On each burst the FIRST action is to capture every item into a visible tracked list and reply with the ordered plan plus what is already in flight; dispatch second. One honest 'captured all ten, here's the order, these three are already running' beats silent parallelism. Acknowledge first, optimise throughput second. (fast-agentic-delivery.md.)
expectations: Keeps parallel dispatch but requires an explicit acknowledgement/plan reply first
Captures every feedback item into a visible tracked list rather than only dispatching
Explains that silent throughput reads as not listening
Orders: acknowledge + plan first, dispatch second

evals.prompt: A subagent I dispatched just sent a task-'completed' notification, but it had armed a background monitor. There's remaining work, so I'll immediately dispatch a second lane into the same worktree to finish it. OK?
evals.expected_output: Confirm the subagent is actually IDLE first. A 'completed' notification is not proof of terminal completion: on a harness that fires 'completed' each time an agent stops with no live background children of its own (and can notify the same task-id more than once), a subagent that armed a background monitor/watch cycles stop->wake and emits 'completed' on each stop -- so a single 'completed' is one of several, not done. The tell: a repeated 'completed' for the same task-id, or the agent's own last report still saying 'waiting.' Check its live state and those tells before dispatching a duplicate into the SAME worktree, where a collision corrupts the run. This is the dispatcher mirror of 'a backgrounded gate loses its verdict' -- there the doer drops a result, here the watcher acts on a not-yet-final one. (fast-agentic-delivery.md.)
expectations: Does not treat a 'completed' notification as proof the subagent is idle, especially with a background monitor armed
Requires confirming the agent's live idle state before dispatching a duplicate
Uses the tell -- a repeated 'completed' for the same task-id, or the agent's report still 'waiting' -- to detect a not-yet-final signal
Flags the same-worktree collision risk

evals.prompt: A background subagent's transcript file hasn't grown in four minutes. I'm going to treat the lane as hung, kill it, and re-dispatch the work. Reasonable?
evals.expected_output: No -- a transcript's size or mtime is not a liveness signal, and killing the lane is a destructive, shared-state action. A transcript can lag a working agent by many minutes (a long tool call, a quiet reasoning stretch, buffered/flushed-late output) and can look equally 'recent' for an agent that already exited -- so a stat-based 'hung' inference cuts both ways: it kills a still-working lane (losing its in-flight work and worktree state) or trusts a dead one. Judge liveness from the agent's ACTUAL product -- a fresh work-tree diff or new commit, a live child process, an owned port/PID, or a direct ping it answers -- not the transcript file's age. Confirm the agent is genuinely idle by a positive signal before terminating (principle 9 -- closing or deleting shared state needs evidence, not presumption). If nothing but the transcript is observable, the honest state is UNVERIFIED, not 'dead.' This is the inverse of the idle-before-duplicate case: a false-negative liveness read leading to a destructive kill, not a false-positive 'completed' leading to a duplicate dispatch. (fast-agentic-delivery.md.)
expectations: Rejects transcript/output-file size or mtime as a liveness signal in either direction
Requires a positive liveness signal (work-tree diff, new commit, live process, owned port/PID, answered ping) before judging the lane
Treats killing a lane as a destructive shared-state action to confirm before, and labels a transcript-only state UNVERIFIED not dead
Distinguishes the destructive false-negative-kill error from the false-positive-completed duplicate-dispatch error

evals.prompt: Our dev server rewrites a tracked config file on boot, and a pre-commit gate asserts that file's exact contents, so every commit fails while the server runs. I keep stopping the server to commit. Better pattern?
evals.expected_output: Serve and commit from separate trees. A long-running process (dev server, codegen/asset watcher) that rewrites a tracked, gate-asserted file on boot keeps that file dirty for its whole lifetime, so every commit from the same working tree fails on a 'modified config' nobody edited -- the stop-server/restore/re-commit dance is the symptom. Give the running stack its own worktree/checkout so the commit tree stays clean; if one tree is unavoidable, make the process write to a gitignored/untracked path, or stop it and restore the file before committing. Where a legitimate tool rewrites the file, prefer a gate that asserts its shape/schema over its exact bytes. This is a single-tree serve-vs-commit deadlock -- distinct from 'never build against a directory a running server is serving' (a stale-asset ship failure) and from out-of-tree scratch crossing commit metadata between lanes. (fast-agentic-delivery.md.)
expectations: Identifies the shared single tree as the root: a running process dirties a tracked, gate-asserted file so the commit gate fails
Recommends serving from a separate worktree/checkout from the one you commit from
Offers the one-tree fallbacks -- gitignore/untrack the rewritten path, or stop-and-restore before commit -- and prefers a schema/shape assertion over exact bytes
Distinguishes the serve-vs-commit deadlock from build-against-served-dir and from out-of-tree-scratch metadata crossing

evals.prompt: An agent is about to start on a feature. The repo's module-ownership map says its lane owns api/, and the GitHub issue for the feature is assigned to it. No draft PR exists, no worktree is open, and there are no commits yet. Is it clear to open a worktree and start building?
evals.expected_output: Not on that evidence alone. The ownership map is a write-lock, not a work-lock: 'this lane owns api/' says who may WRITE api/, not whether someone is already BUILDING this feature (possibly from other files, like web/ or a shared lib). And a forge assignment is intent, not progress -- an assigned issue with no draft PR, no worktree, and no commits is unclaimed in practice (assigned != in-progress). Before opening the worktree, check for an active lane on the OBJECTIVE (not just file ownership): running workers, open/draft PRs, git worktree list. Then announce-then-take -- claim the objective with a draft PR or a posted 'taking this' BEFORE opening the worktree, never after; take-then-announce races two lanes onto the same work. (fast-agentic-delivery.md.)
expectations: Distinguishes the ownership map (write-lock on a file) from a work-lock on the objective
Treats the assignment as intent not progress (assigned != in-progress) given no draft PR/worktree/commits
Requires checking for an active lane on the objective before starting, not just file ownership
Requires announce-then-take: claim the objective before opening the worktree, not after

evals.prompt: I'm sizing a heavy write fan-out on a shared machine. My probe reads 84% free RAM -- comfortable -- so I'm about to spawn three more lanes. (Swap is ~76% consumed but I only glanced once; the session has felt slow and nothing has landed in a while.) Green light?
evals.expected_output: No -- don't spawn. Free-RAM percentage fails open under thrash: it is a post-mitigation number (the OS has already paged out, evicted caches, and compressed memory to relieve pressure), so it reads healthiest exactly when the machine is most degraded. 84% free with swap ~76% consumed and nothing landing is a machine already shedding load. Gate on the SWAP TREND, sampled at least twice seconds apart, on its computed DIRECTION not its level -- swap that is climbing stops the spawn even at high free RAM. Free RAM may corroborate a STOP but must never on its own authorize a SPAWN. And the other two signals here already say stop: the session is slow and nothing has landed -- an observed collapse in work rate IS the resource signal and outranks any green metric. Probe free disk, worktree count, and the live-lane count too (a fan-out sized against memory alone dies of disk), and re-probe before each spawn -- never compute a ceiling once and burst up to it. (fast-agentic-delivery.md.)
expectations: Refuses the spawn despite 84% free RAM; names free-RAM% as a post-mitigation figure that fails open under thrash
Gates on the swap TREND sampled twice (direction, not level); free RAM may corroborate a stop but never authorize a spawn
Treats the slow session / nothing-landing as a work-rate-collapse resource signal that outranks the green metric
Adds free disk, worktree count, and live-lane count to the probe and re-probes before each spawn

evals.prompt: I have one implementation lane running a consolidated deliverable. The owner keeps sending new requirements -- this is the fifth 'also add X' in a couple hours. My instinct is to interrupt the lane and re-brief it each time so its scope stays current. It hasn't produced a branch or commit yet. Right approach?
evals.expected_output: No -- interrupt-and-re-brief is why it has shipped nothing. Each interrupt lands mid-orient and that partial state isn't resumable, so the lane restarts its orientation every time; and each 'also add X' grows scope while retiring nothing, so its definition of done recedes faster than it can implement. Queue new requirements to a durable FILE the lane polls at its own checkpoints (a checklist in the repo or an agreed scratch path), not into an interrupt -- it finishes the unit it's on, then picks up the queue. Reserve interrupts for genuine control signals: stop, abandon, or a correction that invalidates work in progress; 'also do X' is not one. Freeze the scope per deliverable -- later asks are the next increment -- and prefer a shippable slice that then stops over a consolidated deliverable with no stopping point. Finally, the fifth re-brief is itself the signal: more than one or two scope-extending messages means the scope was mis-sized -- split it, don't send a sixth. (fast-agentic-delivery.md.)
expectations: Rejects interrupt-and-re-brief; explains each interrupt restarts orientation and each ask grows scope so done recedes
Queues new scope to a durable file the lane polls at checkpoints, not an interrupt
Reserves interrupts for control signals (stop/abandon/invalidating correction); freezes scope per deliverable, later asks = next increment
Reads the repeated re-briefs as a mis-sized-scope signal -- split the lane, don't send another

evals.prompt: A research lane I commissioned came back with a strong brief -- eight recommendations, well-argued. I pasted it into the thread and moved on to the next task. In my status I'm counting the investigation as a completed deliverable. Is that right?
evals.expected_output: No -- a brief in the transcript is researched, not delivered; its honest status is 'researched, 0 items tracked,' not 'done' (a transcript is not a landed artifact). Research earns its cost only when its conclusions become tracked work, so turn the eight recommendations into an enumerated list and open each as an issue, a backlog row, or a RECORDED REJECTION now, while the context is live -- a conclusion left only in the thread is lost at the next compaction or handoff. Report consumption, not production: what got tracked, not 'I researched X.' Check the depth distribution before calling it consumed -- if only the cheap, obvious items would ever get opened and the expensive structural ones evaporate, the value you commissioned did not land. And name the downstream consumer the brief was for; if a loop keeps commissioning briefs while the thing they were meant to unblock never moves, research is displacing delivery. (fast-agentic-delivery.md.)
expectations: Rejects counting the brief as a completed deliverable -- a transcript is not a landed artifact; status is 'researched, 0 tracked'
Requires each recommendation become a tracked item (issue/backlog row/recorded rejection) opened in the same step, while context is live
Reports consumption not production; checks the depth distribution (not only cheap items landing)
Names the downstream consumer; flags research displacing the delivery it was meant to inform

evals.prompt: I told three parallel lanes to each 'work in an isolated worktree off the integration branch.' The integrator lane merged a finished lane, verified everything in the running app, then npm test failed on a half-written test file it never created -- another lane had been writing into the same checkout. git worktree add for the integration branch refuses because it's already checked out. Should the integrator just stash the stray file and push its verified merge?
evals.expected_output: No -- stashing another lane's uncommitted work removes it silently and is unrecoverable from that lane's side; that is data loss to paper over a coordination bug. The real fault is the brief: 'an isolated worktree off X' is an adjective, not an assignment, so two lanes collided on the tree (not on any file -- their file sets were disjoint). Fixes: (1) give each lane an exact path it alone writes under (<scratch>/wt-<lane>); (2) the integrator folds in on a DETACHED worktree -- git worktree add --detach <path> <branch> (the local branch tip, not origin/<branch>, so it lands on the just-verified merge and does not fail on a local-only integration branch), merge, verify, publish, remove -- which is immune to the 'already checked out' refusal and cannot be squatted, with how it publishes (a direct push or a PR, under whatever publish gate the project applies) left as a separate choice; (3) before writing, run git status --short on the target tree and stop if it shows changes the lane did not make -- foreign dirt means the tree is occupied; (4) read the failing test in an untouched file as an environment fault, not a code fault -- re-run it in a clean or detached tree before chasing a bug that is not there. The verified merge itself is fine; it just has to be published from a tree the integrator actually owns. (fast-agentic-delivery.md.)
expectations: Refuses to stash the foreign file -- silent, unrecoverable data loss for the other lane; names the ambiguous brief as root cause (collision on the tree, not a file)
Integrator uses a detached worktree (git worktree add --detach <branch>, the local tip) to escape the already-checked-out refusal; assigns each lane an exact path
Verifies tree ownership (git status --short) before writing and stops on foreign changes
Classifies the failing test in an untouched file as an environment fault to re-run in a clean tree, not a code bug to chase

evals.prompt: I kicked off the full verification lane (browser suite + prod build + 26-route audit) against the integration branch while eight feature lanes were still folding in. It came back pass on head A, but the head is now A+8. Can I report 'verified, ready to ship'?
evals.expected_output: No -- that verdict certifies a tree that no longer exists (tested A, head is A+8); it is not exactly wrong, it is about something else, and reporting it as 'verified' is worse than no verdict because it gets quoted downstream as certification. Release verification and defect discovery run the same commands but are different contracts: discovery runs continuously during integration against any recent head and its DEFECTS stay useful even when stale; release verification certifies ONE frozen head, once, after integration closes, and a stale verification verdict certifies nothing. So harvest the real defects that run surfaced as LEADS and re-confirm each at the new head A+8 before fixing (a finding carried forward without a re-run is unverified, not still-open), but DISCARD its pass/fail -- do not file it as certification. Re-run release verification only once the integrator reports no outstanding branches (quiescent); record and re-check the SHA (report STALE -- tested <sha>, head is now <sha> if it moved, never a bare pass/fail); give the heavy run the machine so it does not starve into a no-result stall; and split it (unit/type/lint -> browser -> audit -> preflight) so a stall does not lose the earlier phases. (fast-agentic-delivery.md.)
expectations: Refuses to report the stale verdict as certification -- it tested A, head is A+8; a verdict without a current SHA certifies nothing
Separates defect discovery (findings durable as LEADS, re-confirmed at the new head; verdict disposable) from release verification (one frozen head); harvests defects, discards the pass/fail
Re-runs release verification only on a quiescent head (integrator reports no outstanding branches), freezing and naming the SHA
Gives the heavy run the machine and splits it into independently-reporting phases so partial progress survives

evals.prompt: My agent coordinator has a ranked backlog of disjoint-surface tasks, the box is at 83% free RAM with flat swap, and the owner hasn't messaged in a while. Right now, each time a lane finishes I just acknowledge it and wait for the owner's next message before launching more -- the owner is annoyed I keep slowing down when they go quiet. Also, earlier a different run spawned ~246 worktrees, used 99 GB, and stalled everything. What's the right admission policy?
evals.expected_output: Two failures to fix at once -- do not trade one for the other. First: the owner's message cadence is not your clock. Acknowledging a completed lane one-for-one and waiting for the next message makes human message frequency an accidental concurrency controller, so throughput sags exactly when the owner is quiet while safe capacity (83% free RAM, flat swap) sits idle. A completed lane refills on YOUR own cadence: hold target concurrency while eligible backlog and headroom remain, and a quiet stretch never lowers it. Second, and simultaneously: admission is bounded, not unlimited -- the 246-worktree / 99 GB stall is the inverse failure. So maintain a TARGET concurrency with gradual admission (add one lane, re-probe free RAM and the swap trend, then decide on the next) plus backpressure; admit only disjoint-surface lanes (a shared artifact in flight blocks only the lanes that touch it, not the disjoint ones); and stop admitting when swap rises or headroom/disk runs low -- never keying admission to message count. Refill on quiet AND stop at the resource ceiling -- both, or you have only moved the failure. (fast-agentic-delivery.md.)
expectations: Refills each vacated slot on the coordinator's own cadence while backlog + headroom remain; a quiet period never lowers target concurrency; admission is not keyed to owner-message count
Admits gradually (add one lane, re-probe free RAM + swap trend, decide) and only for disjoint surfaces (a shared artifact in flight blocks only lanes that touch it)
Bounds concurrency -- stops admission on rising swap / low headroom; names the 246-worktree / 99 GB stall as the inverse failure to avoid
Holds BOTH halves at once (refill on quiet AND stop at the ceiling), not one at the expense of the other

evals.prompt: In a 7-hour unattended run the owner has asked 'how much is left?' six times. Each time my agent re-reads about a thousand lines of transcript to rebuild the list, and a couple of items got re-done because their 'done' status was based on a branch existing. We already run an end-of-session reconciliation. What's missing?
evals.expected_output: The end-of-session reconciliation is a run-once, review-side audit -- it does not fix MID-session drift, which is your actual failure. The durable backlog the loop already keeps must ALSO be indexed by the owner's ask-set: one row per distinct request (id, ask, status, evidence, next action), updated at each milestone, not only at the end. 'What's remaining' is then answered by READING that ledger -- one or two tool calls -- never by an O(N) re-scan of the transcript that silently re-litigates settled items. And a row is done only when its evidence points at the CANONICAL surface (a merged-to-default SHA or a live URL), not a branch that merely contains the fix -- project-state.md's receipt discipline (a checkpoint is a recorded claim, not evidence). The fix is not another audit; it is making the ledger a live, ask-indexed, read-first artifact. (fast-agentic-delivery.md.)
expectations: Names mid-session drift as distinct from the end-of-session / review-side reconciliation, which does not fix it
Requires the durable backlog to carry the ask-set (one row per owner request) updated at each milestone
Answers 'what's left' by reading the ledger in one or two tool calls, not by re-scanning the transcript
Marks a row done only on the canonical surface (merged-to-default SHA / live URL), not branch existence -- links project-state.md receipt discipline

evals.prompt: I'm coordinating a lane that's mid-way through filing an issue and drafting a PR. I keep realizing better process: first I told it serial, then adaptive-parallel, then priority-first ordering -- three redirects in a few minutes. It hasn't shipped anything yet. Am I improving the process or hurting it?
evals.expected_output: Hurting it -- this is interrupt-thrash. Each mid-task redirect makes the lane re-orient and restart, so three policy changes in minutes guarantee zero output; the coordinator feels like it is improving the process while the lane is reset to zero each time. A process-policy change -- queue order, serial vs parallel, reprioritization -- is NOT a control signal (nor is 'also do X'): it queues to the lane's next CHECKPOINT (a filed issue, a pushed commit, a merged PR -- never a mid-edit / mid-compose state). A genuine control signal -- stop, abandon, or a correction that invalidates the work (a P0 safety issue: imminent data loss, a secret leak, or a destructive irreversible action, is the clearest case) -- still interrupts at once; a process-policy change is not one and waits. Let the lane reach its checkpoint, apply one batched policy update there, and if a lane has taken more than one or two redirects without completing, that is the signal the scope was mis-sized -- stop sending and let it ship. (fast-agentic-delivery.md.)
expectations: Names interrupt-thrash: rapid mid-task redirects reset the lane to zero, so throughput is zero despite each redirect being individually reasonable
A process-policy change (ordering / parallelism / priority) is not a control signal; it queues to the next checkpoint

Defines the checkpoint (filed issue / pushed commit / merged PR, not mid-edit); a process-policy change waits for it, while a genuine control signal (stop / abandon / a work-invalidating correction such as a P0 safety issue) still interrupts at once
Stops sending after more than one or two uncompleted redirects rather than sending a third

evals.prompt: I reported to the owner '4 lanes working, ETA 20 min.' All 4 are computing locally -- none has pushed a commit or opened a PR yet. Two later stalled and reset. The owner's annoyed the ETA was wrong. What did I get wrong?
evals.expected_output: The ETA counted spawned lanes as progress. A lane computing locally with nothing pushed is, to the owner, in the same state as one never spawned -- spawned is not started (the claim-side form is 'assigned is not in-progress'). Grade each lane on durable output: zero (local only, no push -- not-started however long it has run), in-flight (a pushed branch or open draft PR -- visible, recoverable), done (merged to the default branch or a filed issue). A status names each lane's push / PR / issue URL; a lane with no URL is 'running, no output yet,' never progress. Project the window's ETA from the durable-output RATE, not the spawn rate -- otherwise it is fiction the moment a local lane stalls or resets, which is exactly what happened. Report '0 of 4 durable, none pushed yet' instead of '4 working, ETA 20 min.' (fast-agentic-delivery.md.)
expectations: Names the error: counting spawned/local-only lanes as progress; spawned is not started
Grades lanes by durable output (zero / in-flight / done) tied to a pushed artifact, not lane count or elapsed time
Requires the status to name each lane's push/PR/issue URL; no URL = 'running, no output yet'
Derives ETA from the durable-output rate, not the spawn rate

evals.prompt: The conductor is about to dispatch a lane that makes paid model calls, but no per-lane token/dollar budget was set at G2. The team says 'just run it, we will watch the cost.' What does the gate require?
evals.expected_output: G2's hard condition is that every lane with a paid model call names a per-lane token/dollar budget before G4 -- so a lane with NO budget set is BLOCKED, not run unlimited (a cap that defaults to off is not a cap; 'we will watch the cost' is not a budget). Two co-equal invariants apply and are not substitutes: missing spend cap is BLOCKED, never unlimited (the budget is the bound itself), and missing price is UNPRICED, never reported as zero (label the cost honestly). Block the dispatch until a per-lane budget is set at G2; do not let it run on 'we will watch.' (agentic-delivery SKILL.md G2 + the UNVERIFIED/UNPRICED/BLOCKED rule.)
expectations: A paid-model-call lane with no per-lane budget set is BLOCKED, not run unlimited ('we will watch the cost' is not a budget; a cap defaulting to off is not a cap)
Missing price is reported UNPRICED, never as zero -- honest cost labeling, distinct from the budget bound
The budget (the bound) and the UNPRICED label are not substitutes -- both apply
Blocks the dispatch until a per-lane token/dollar budget is set at G2

evals.prompt: You are designing the primary surface of a product whose value is how companies, people, and deals connect. A builder proposes a flat sortable table of companies as the landing view, with the relationships available two clicks into each record. What does the build-side product playbook say, and how is that choice verified?
evals.expected_output: Lead with the relationship, not the record. When the product's value is in how entities connect, the primary surface makes the relationship the first-class object -- the path between two entities, the shared context, the chain of dependence. A flat entity table with the connections buried inverts the value proposition: it fronts the records a user could get anywhere and hides the graph that is the reason to use the product. Build the relationship as the entry view; record detail is the drill-down. This is a G3 Design build choice recorded in the ADR; deep-code-review domain P verifies it at G6 review (a surface that buries its own core value reads as low actionability). The playbook does not restate domain P's review axes -- it points to product-ux-quality.md for the shared ones (why-it-matters, ranking, progressive disclosure, one-component, interaction-completeness) and adds only the build-time patterns domain P does not shape. (agentic-delivery production-grade-product-playbook.md.)
expectations: Says lead with the relationship / connection as the first-class object, not a flat entity table with the relationships buried
Names the inversion: a record table fronts what is available anywhere and hides the graph that is the product's actual value
Ties it to the gates: chosen at G3 Design (recorded in the ADR), verified by deep-code-review domain P at G6
Notes the playbook points to product-ux-quality.md for the shared review axes rather than restating them (no duplication)

evals.prompt: An agent fleet merges day-to-day into a long-lived `development` branch and promotes to `main` (the default branch) weekly. The conductor sees issue #500 still OPEN and is about to spawn a lane to implement its fix. The issue has a merged PR whose body said 'Closes #500.' What should happen before laning?
evals.expected_output: Do not treat OPEN as proof the fix is absent. GitHub auto-close is default-branch-only -- a linked issue closes only when a linked PR merges into the default branch, and the Closes/Fixes/Resolves #N keywords are interpreted only when the PR targets the default branch. A fleet merging into `development` therefore leaves issues 'done in the tree, open in the tracker.' Before laning: (1) grep the branch you would actually base the fix on -- the integration branch (`development`), not the issue state -- for the fix's landmark (the changed symbol, line, or the regression test that guards it); (2) cross-reference the integration branch's commit log and the merged PR. If the fix is already on `development`: STOP, report 'already delivered' with file:line + the commit SHA, note it is on the integration branch but not yet on the default branch (so the open issue is expected -- it does NOT auto-close on convergence: the Closes #N was inert because it did not target the default branch, and the promotion PR carries no per-issue keyword, so it closes only via a keyword-linked PR to the default branch or a supplied automation), do NOT re-lane, and do NOT hand-close it ('done' means merged to the default branch). This is the duplicate-work failure one level up from re-searching for code already present. (fast-agentic-delivery.md.)
expectations: Recognizes OPEN is not proof the fix is absent -- GitHub auto-close (Closes #N) fires only on the default branch, so an off-default merge leaves the issue open
Before laning, greps the actual integration/base branch for the fix's landmark (symbol/line/regression test), not just the issue state
If already delivered on the integration branch: stop and report 'already delivered' with file:line + commit SHA; do not re-lane
Does NOT hand-close the issue -- 'done' means merged to the default branch

evals.prompt: Our CI fails a PR if the whole repo exceeds an absolute `--max-warnings 40` ceiling. It worked fine for one committer, but now that we fan work out to several parallel build lanes, a lane sometimes goes red for a warning it didn't introduce. What's happening, and what should the gate be?
evals.expected_output: An absolute count over the whole tree is a shared counter, and parallel lanes each rebased from the same base are blind to each other's deltas: lane A lands and consumes the last slot, then lane B -- whose own diff is no worse -- pushes and trips N+1, red for arriving second. The failure scales with fan-out width and is invisible until the second lane's CI runs (the first lane saw only headroom). Fix: gate on the per-diff delta -- 'this change introduces no new warnings versus its merge base' -- which is order-independent, so no lane can consume another's slot; keep the absolute count only as a slow-moving burndown target (a report or a non-blocking trend), never the per-PR gate under fan-out. Also brief every lane to fix any warning its own diff introduces before pushing, and never raise the ceiling to pass (a ratchet only tightens). Same shape for any absolute-threshold gate on a shared counter -- a coverage-percent floor, a bundle-size budget: under concurrency, gate on the delta the change owns, not the tree total. (Distinct from a `--max-warnings` false-fail caused by a symlinked dep tree inflating the count -- that is an infra 'could not run' where the count is wrong, not contended.) (agentic-delivery/references/fast-agentic-delivery.md.)
expectations: Identifies the absolute tree-wide count as contended shared state -- parallel lanes off the same base are blind to each other's deltas, so the second to push trips the ceiling for a diff no worse than the first (punished for arriving second)
Prescribes gating on the per-diff delta ('no new warnings versus the merge base') and notes it is order-independent, so no lane consumes another's slot
Keeps the absolute count only as a slow-moving burndown target, never the per-PR gate under fan-out; and never raise the ceiling to pass (a ratchet only tightens)
Generalizes to any absolute-threshold gate on a shared counter (coverage %, bundle-size) -- under concurrency gate on the delta the change owns
Distinguishes this (count right but contended) from the phantom-warning false-fail where a symlinked dep tree makes the count wrong (an infra 'could not run')
